community.name: Cyber Defense Indonesia
community.description: Community members show the tools they vibe-coded on nights and weekends: personal projects, side quests, and things built because something annoyed them enough.

episodes.title: Vibe coding show & tell
episodes.summary: Four security-minded builders demoed what they made with AI coding agents: an anti-scam checker for our parents, a private OSINT graph, a phishing sandbox that sees what public scanners miss, and a credibility meter for the posts clogging your feed. Along the way the panel traded notes on model routing, spec-driven development, token budgets and guardrails.

chapters.label: Closing: is vibe coding creating value?

takeaways: Plan with a big model, execute with a small one. A clear plan.md lets a cheaper model implement it without burning context on file reads.
Keep planning and execution in separate sessions so the execution context isn't already full of planning chatter.
If you keep hitting the same wall, start a new session with a sharper prompt instead of arguing with the agent.
Write the requirements yourself and review them line by line. Trust the agent more as you move from design to tasks.
Prompt caching varies a lot between providers and it shows up directly in cost.
When a model's guardrails block legitimate security work, switch models rather than jailbreak an account you care about.
A weekend project doesn't need enterprise architecture. Choose serverless and cheap models and accept an A graded as a B.
Learn the fundamentals. You can't review what the AI wrote if you don't understand the infrastructure it chose.

episodes.title: CDEF Vibe Coding Showcase #2
episodes.summary: Three presenters, four tools. A URL scanner and threat-intel hub tuned for the Indonesian internet, a scam simulator that trains your instincts instead of asking you to memorise every trick, a 10-minute account-hardening guide built in a weekend after a wave of hacked creator accounts, and an autonomous monitor that watches GitHub, npm, PyPI and RubyGems for malicious packages. The episode closes with a real fake-job lure: a Go take-home project with a stealer hidden in its Git hooks.

chapters.label: Case study: the fake job with a poisoned Git hook

takeaways: Validate the idea before writing code. Cross-check it with several chat models and ask them to score feasibility, whether the problem is real, and whether you're the right person to solve it.
AI drifts into yes-man mode over long sessions. Tell it plainly not to affirm your ideas, and stay critical yourself.
Ship an MVP to a few trusted people, then launch. You won't get it perfect on day one, and endless polishing is its own failure mode.
Check AI-generated names and logos before you launch. One project's AI-made logo turned out to match an existing trademark.
For content that goes stale, schedule an agent to compare your pages against trusted sources and send you the gaps, with a human approving each change.
Write a spec before you let the agent code. A clear spec saves tokens and rework.
When AI writes the code, spend the time you save on securing it: test locally, ask the agent to hunt for OWASP-style bugs, and scan before each big deploy.
Coding agents install packages too. Gate installs with a hook that checks OSV for known malicious packages.
Never run a recruiter's take-home project on your own laptop. Open it in a sandbox and read .git/hooks first.

projects.name: Ponten
projects.tagline: Check a suspicious link, phone number or bank account before you click or transfer.
projects.summary: A mobile-first scam checker in plain Indonesian, made for people outside security, especially parents and older relatives who get a sketchy WhatsApp, SMS or Telegram message and don't know who to ask.
projects.problem: Scam links like klikbca.id vs klikbca.com are easy to miss if you aren't in security. Existing checkers are built for analysts, not for the family group chat.
features: Screenshot check: upload a photo of a suspicious chat and AI reads the message and points out what's off
Link check against several OSINT sources, with a clear verdict and the reason behind it, such as a very new domain
Phone and bank account check, backed by community reports (no government API yet, so treat unknowns with care)
Scam-awareness quiz with seven real-world scenarios
Community scam reports, each one reviewed by hand
Works without an account (rate-limited); sign in to keep your check history
Coming later: hoax-news lookup against fact-checkers, and a check for AI-generated photos and video
projects.howItWasBuilt: Built over roughly a month of casual evenings with Claude Code on Opus. Rizal leaned on subagents playing architect, code reviewer, security reviewer and tester, and used skills to break the build into steps, while keeping an eye on context: loading too many skills in one session filled it quickly.
projects.privacy: Only the screenshots are kept, cached for about 24 hours and then deleted. Nothing else sensitive is stored, which keeps it in the spirit of Indonesia's PDP law.
lessons: Claude is token-hungry once you add agents and skills: one feature can use up a session, and then you wait around 5 hours for the limit to reset.
Plan early and revisit the plan in MD files so the next session, or a different model, can pick up where you stopped.
roadmap: Hoax-news check
AI-generated image and video detection
Compare the workflow against OpenCode and cheaper models

projects.name: OSINT Graph Mapper
projects.tagline: Map entities, relationships and evidence in a local, encrypted vault. Nothing is uploaded.
projects.summary: A browser-only investigation workspace for OSINT. You build a graph of people, domains, accounts and wallets, attach evidence to any node or link, and everything stays encrypted on your own device.
projects.problem: Graph tools like Maltego are powerful, but they're licensed per seat and your queries travel through someone else's servers. For sensitive or confidential investigations, the goal was for the analyst to be the only one holding the data, with a UI that doesn't fight you.
features: Interactive graph with typed relationships and 92 entity types, from domain, ASN and wallet to person, email and social accounts
Service registry (GitHub, Telegram, X and more) so account nodes resolve to the right platform
Evidence board: attach URLs, notes, documents and citations to an entity, a relationship or the whole case
Per-node metadata: source, confidence score (0–100), verification status and analyst notes
TLP classification, per-case passwords and auto-lock after inactivity
Encrypted backups to a file, WebDAV or S3, all without a backend
Exports and handoff: graph PNG, Markdown report, and a passphrase-protected bundle with the reports, graph, manifest and encrypted backup
Command palette and keyboard shortcuts for quickly adding nodes and sub-nodes
projects.howItWasBuilt: It started as a regular app with a Postgres backend. Aan then asked how anyone could trust that their data was safe on a database the author controls, and rebuilt it as client-side only, which meant the frontend had to cover every feature. Aan works across a mix of agents and models, sending cheap models like DeepSeek Flash, MiMo or GLM to explore the codebase and saving bigger ones for implementation.
projects.privacy: Cases are encrypted at rest in IndexedDB with a key derived by PBKDF2 (about 250k iterations) and AES-GCM. The hosted site only serves the UI. There's no password recovery by design, and clearing your browser data deletes your cases, so keep backups.
lessons: No model is simply bad. What matters is giving each one the right role: cheap models for exploring, strong models for implementing.
Never plan and execute in the same session. Write a plan.md, then run it in a fresh one.
Choose providers with good prompt caching. DeepSeek's cache hits make long sessions far cheaper.
Codex and ChatGPT are the most sensitive to guardrails for security tooling. Switch models rather than risk a ban on an important account.
Small models need concrete constraints (framework, database, structure). The more detail you give, the faster you get there.
roadmap: Maltego import
Embedding evidence files (base64) instead of linking by URL
Better report export

projects.name: Phishing Analyzer
projects.tagline: A self-hosted phishing sandbox that sees what public scanners miss.
projects.summary: Paste a URL and it opens the page as a phone would, from wherever you deploy it. It then asks an AI model for a verdict, queries ten threat-intel sources in parallel, and drafts the takedown email for you.
projects.problem: Modern phishing kits cloak themselves. They only render on mobile browsers, block visitors from the wrong country, and some even check the phone's language. Public scanners run from US or EU desktops and see a harmless page. Pasting a customer-targeted URL into public scanners also leaks the investigation.
features: Headless Chromium through Playwright, emulating an iPhone 14, captures a full-page mobile screenshot
AI vision verdict (phishing, suspicious, legitimate or inconclusive) with a confidence score and the brand being impersonated. It can translate foreign-language lures too
Ten optional intel sources queried in parallel: URLScan, VirusTotal, Shodan, Censys, Google Safe Browsing, OTX, AbuseIPDB, crt.sh, URLhaus and PhishTank
Deploy it in any region, such as a VPS in the target country or the EU for GDPR, to choose where the scan comes from
Hunting and pivot hints: other domains on the same IP, lookalike domains and TLS certificate details
RDAP-based takedown report with registrar and hosting abuse contacts filled in, plus a one-click Google Safe Browsing report
Searchable case history for the whole team, with dark and light modes
projects.howItWasBuilt: It was built to fix a specific problem at work: phishing aimed at users in another country that only opened with a local IP and a local-language phone. It runs on one Ubuntu VPS behind a simple password, and the AI provider can be switched to Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, OpenAI, OpenRouter or any OpenAI-compatible model such as DeepSeek. The demo didn't say which coding agent was used to build it.
projects.privacy: Scans come from your own infrastructure, so nothing appears in public scan feeds. Third-party intel lookups are optional if you don't want your URLs shared.
lessons: Build the tool for the gap you actually have. Here that was geo-fenced, mobile-only phishing that public sandboxes can't see.
Adding an API is almost free with vibe coding, and it's the path into SOAR or Jira automation so analysts never need to open the UI.
roadmap: API for SOAR and Jira Automation
Video capture of scripted interaction
Amazon Linux support
Automated takedown

projects.name: Fishymeter
projects.tagline: Everything's fishy. Score any post, article, image or PDF for credibility before you trust it.
projects.summary: A credibility meter for the confident, unsourced, AI-written posts all over LinkedIn and Instagram. It scores content on six dimensions it can judge from the content alone, and you can use it to check your own writing before you post.
projects.problem: People who aren't technical tend to take a polished infographic at face value. Real fact-checking needs either a model that knows more than the author (correctness) or cited sources to compare against (faithfulness), and most posts offer neither. Fishymeter checks whether a piece is worth your time rather than whether it's true.
features: Six self-contained scoring dimensions: accuracy (does it stay on topic), internal consistency, source attribution, bias, originality and transparency (who wrote it, and was AI disclosed)
Bias and originality are weighted lower, because an AWS employee praising AWS is expected when they say so openly
Grades from Rare Catch and Fresh Catch down to Rotten Fish and Dead Fish
Accepts pasted text (up to 2,000 words), a URL, or a PNG, JPEG or PDF (up to 5 MB)
Your catches are private by default. Publish one to share its analysis, or browse the week's top-scored public catches
Sign in with email or Google, up to 100 analyses a day
projects.howItWasBuilt: A weekend project built spec-first in Kiro: requirements, then design, then a task list, with every commit tied to a task so the next weekend starts exactly where the last one ended. Kiro runs on an EC2 instance and Resa drives it from Slack by phone, then closes the laptop and lets it work through the tasks overnight.
projects.privacy: Uploaded originals are kept for 30 days. The model ID and features live in config and feature flags, so they can be swapped without a redeploy. The whole thing runs for about $3 a month.
lessons: Write the requirements yourself and review them 100%. Review the design around 75%, and let the agent own the tasks.
Requirements are a living document. Add them block by block, such as moving scoring to AgentCore before adding browsing.
Don't treat a vibe-coded side project like an enterprise product. Pick serverless and a cheap model, and accept an A graded as a B as long as an A never gets an F.
On a team, agree on one spec workflow and one set of skills, or everyone's commits will point at different artifacts.
roadmap: Expose scoring as an MCP server so you can check a draft from your editor
Open-source it after a security review

projects.name: InsightURL
projects.tagline: A URL scanner and threat-intel hub built for the Indonesian internet.
projects.summary: It started as a personal urlscan.io clone and grew into a toolkit for anyone defending Indonesian users and brands: scan a link without opening it, check whether a lender is licensed, see who is impersonating a brand, and follow the threats aimed at Indonesia.
projects.problem: Global scanners and paid threat-intel platforms rarely go deep on Indonesia. They won't tell you whether a site is registered as a PSE with Komdigi, whether a pinjol is on the OJK list, or which local brands are being impersonated this week.
features: URL scan with screenshot, certificate, headers, DNS, redirects and phishing signals, plus an A–F hygiene grade with a plain explanation of what it means
Brand directory and impostor watch for Indonesian brands, with email alerts (instant or daily) when lookalike domains or impersonation appear
Komdigi PSE registration check and an OJK pinjol directory check
Email header analyzer that runs in the browser, plus checks for phone numbers, bank accounts and whole SMS or WhatsApp messages
AI key exposure check that spots provider API keys shipped to visitors in front-end code
Advanced scan with a downloadable HAR file, JavaScript endpoints, credential-pattern matching and a favicon hash ready to paste into Shodan
Threat feeds and reports, ransomware watch for Indonesian victims, a scam feed from Mastodon and Bluesky, QRIS checks, and gambling SEO-injection recon
Recon tools: subdomains from certificate logs, lookalike domains, email and DNS posture, and domain footprint
projects.howItWasBuilt: Riyan plans with ChatGPT and writes the code with Claude Code on Opus and Fable. An Obsidian vault works as the agent's second brain, recording what each version already contains. New features ship as versioned zip patches that are extracted onto shared PHP hosting. Everything is tested locally first, including asking the agent to hunt for OWASP Top 10 bugs and PHP-specific issues, and a small built-in SIEM watches for people probing the site.
projects.privacy: Scans are fetched by the server, not your device, and private address ranges are refused. Deeper checks only run on domains you prove you control. Reports expire, temporary email addresses are blocked at sign-up, and the email header analyzer never leaves your browser.
lessons: Vibe coding made learning addictive: research papers that used to be out of reach become tools you can actually build and share.
Build from what you've learned and researched, not from a one-line wish. The quality of the tool follows the depth of the research.
Some data sources, such as the OJK directory, are still too heavy to refresh automatically, so expect a few manual chores.
roadmap: One-click Shodan links from the favicon hash
More accurate brand-risk scoring
Moving off shared hosting to a VPS

projects.name: ntardulu
projects.tagline: Realistic scam simulations that train you to say "wait a minute" before you click.
projects.summary: A free, no-login scam simulator in Indonesian. You play through a fake WhatsApp chat, SMS, call or search result that looks just like the real thing, make a choice, and then see the red flags you missed and the safe way to check.
projects.problem: After years of awareness content, Marcel noticed a side effect: some people, including Marcel's own mother, became too scared to use mobile banking at all. Memorising every scam script doesn't scale either, because scammers keep the same moves and change the story. What does work is the instinct security people have, and simulations can train that.
features: Over 30 scam simulations drawn from Indonesian cases, across WhatsApp, SMS, calls, email, Instagram, QRIS and Google results
Full-screen, phone-style scenes designed for mobile so they feel like the real thing
Every scenario offers the scammer's path and safer choices, such as closing the chat and opening the real banking app
Credentials are auto-filled in the fake forms, so nobody types a real PIN by accident
A debrief after each run that maps the message back to four hooks: urgency, bait, impersonation and a request for something (OTP, card, data)
Simulations of newer tricks, such as fake bank call centres planted through SEO poisoning and a blue tick that is no longer proof
projects.howItWasBuilt: The code is 100% AI-generated with Claude Code on Opus, after a short trial of Codex. The idea took four to five months of brainstorming across ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, with each one asked to score the idea on feasibility, whether it's a real problem for Indonesians, and whether Marcel was the right person to build it. Early versions went to friends and relatives chosen to cover different age groups before the public launch.
projects.privacy: No sign-up and no personal data. Only anonymous usage is tracked, to learn which scenarios fool people most.
lessons: Your first public product won't be perfect. At one point Claude itself pointed out that the scores had been 9-plus for months and asked what was really stopping the launch.
Feedback on design is contradictory. Ship, then iterate on the comments that make sense.
Expect harsh comments when you launch in public, and ask calmly what's behind them before acting.
roadmap: Detect, respond and recover tools to follow the protect stage
A game-like version that teaches digital safety to children and teenagers

projects.name: MainAman
projects.tagline: Ten minutes of guided steps to lock down the phone, email and apps you actually use.
projects.summary: Pick your devices, email, browser and apps, and MainAman gives you the five most important protections first, each with a simulated walkthrough and a link to the official guide. A separate SOS section helps people whose account has already been hacked.
projects.problem: People constantly asked Marcel how to turn on two-factor authentication on Instagram or set a WhatsApp PIN. Then a wave of hacked creator and public-figure accounts was used to sell fake gold and iPhones, and followers lost money. The fix was already in official help pages, but nobody could find or follow it.
features: Choose from 18 platforms, including Android, iOS, Gmail, Outlook, Chrome, Windows, macOS, WhatsApp, Instagram, TikTok, X and YouTube
Five quick wins picked for you first, so the list doesn't overwhelm
Step-by-step simulated screens showing exactly where each setting lives, with a link to the official guide
A track for creators and social media admins
An SOS section with official recovery paths when an account has already been hacked
projects.howItWasBuilt: The beta was built over a weekend in two to three days with AI coding tools, reusing the simulation idea from ntardulu. It launched quickly after an e-commerce account with a big following offered to help spread it. A Hermes agent checks trusted sources every three days and messages Marcel on WhatsApp when a link or step has changed, and Marcel approves each update before it goes live.
projects.privacy: No sign-up and no personal data stored.
lessons: The hard part of a guide isn't the code but keeping the content current across dozens of platforms. Automate the checking, and keep a human in the loop for changes.
Check AI-generated branding. The first name and AI-made logo, amanin.now, turned out to match a registered brand, so it was renamed to MainAman.
Speed matters when there's an active wave of attacks. A good-enough guide that ships this weekend helps more people than a perfect one next month.
roadmap: Ways to keep people motivated to finish every recommendation

projects.name: PakMon Intel
projects.tagline: An autonomous watchtower for malicious packages on GitHub, npm, PyPI and RubyGems.
projects.summary: PakMon (package monitoring) Intel is like a SIEM for the software supply chain. It listens to every push and release across four ecosystems, triages each change, and sends anything suspicious to an LLM for deep code analysis. You review the alert, then report the package to get it taken down.
projects.problem: A compromised library usually isn't noticed until after people have installed it, and auto-updates pull the poisoned version onto developer laptops, where stealers do their damage. Few researchers talk openly about where supply-chain telemetry comes from or how to analyse it.
features: Listens to change events from GitHub, npm, PyPI and RubyGems, using free endpoints within their rate limits

Two triage modes: deterministic local rules (such as curl or wget piped into a shell, scheduled-task persistence, PowerShell with execution-policy bypass) or a hosted AI classifier that scores each change
Changes above the threshold go to DeepSeek for deep analysis, then back through the classifier for a verdict: malicious, suspicious or benign
About 16,000 packages analysed so far, with findings grouped as remote execution, obfuscation and credential theft
Live activity view of what is being pulled and scanned
SBOM mode in development, to monitor only the dependencies your product uses (or a manual list) and cut costs
Report helper for GitHub and the OpenSSF malicious-packages and OSV databases. One finding has already been taken down from PyPI
projects.howItWasBuilt: Written in Go. Brainstorming happened in ChatGPT with an instruction to skip all affirmation and just give an honest opinion. Because Rei comes from software engineering, the brainstorm's output was already a spec, and Codex built the project from that spec. Claude was too expensive for this.
projects.privacy: Watches public package registries only. Every alert is reviewed by a human before anything is reported.
lessons: Generate a tidy spec first (goals, framework, constraints) and then hand it to the coding agent. It saves tokens.
With AI writing the code, a developer's time shifts to securing it, which is a whole new body of knowledge to learn.

Developers' own laptops are the soft target now, through dependencies, coding agents installing packages, and fake take-home tests. One defence is a hook that checks every library an agent wants to install against OSV first.
The classifier is a proof of concept that rule-based triage can give way to classification. Its verdicts are being collected to train a cheaper in-house model.
roadmap: Public release for education
Finish SBOM monitoring
Train an in-house ML classifier to replace the paid one
Feed in known-malicious sample repos to test detection
